export type User = {
  id: string;
  email: string;
  name: string;
  createdAt: string;
};

const users: User[] = [
  { id: "1", email: "ada@example.com", name: "Ada", createdAt: "2026-01-04" },
  { id: "2", email: "grace@example.com", name: "Grace", createdAt: "2026-02-11" },
];

export async function listUsers(): Promise<User[]> {
  return users;
}

export async function getUser(id: string): Promise<User | undefined> {
  return users.find((u) => u.id === id);
}

// TODO: there is no real session handling yet — the dashboard just picks the first user.
export async function getCurrentUser(): Promise<User | undefined> {
  return users[0];
}

content.content:
# Postmark — transactional email for Next.js Postmark sends an app's transactional email (welcome emails, password resets, receipts) with high delivery rates, bounce and spam processing, and detailed statistics. The official Node.js library `postmark` covers the whole Postmark REST API, uses the native Fetch API and has no runtime dependencies (Node 18+). ## Install ```bash npm install postmark ``` ## 1. Environment variables `.env.local`: ``` POSTMARK_SERVER_TOKEN=server_token_placeholder POSTMARK_FROM_EMAIL=hello@example.com ``` The server token belongs to one Postmark server (Servers → API Tokens). The From address must be a confirmed sender signature or sit on a verified domain. ## 2. Create a client `src/lib/postmark.ts`: ```ts import { ServerClient } from "postmark"; export const postmark = new ServerClient(process.env.POSTMARK_SERVER_TOKEN!); ``` Use the client only in server code (route handlers, server actions, server components). Never expose the server token to the browser. ## 3. Send an email ```ts import { postmark } from "@/lib/postmark"; await postmark.sendEmail({ From: process.env.POSTMARK_FROM_EMAIL!, To: "user@example.com", Subject: "Welcome!", HtmlBody: "

Thanks for signing up.

", TextBody: "Thanks for signing up.", MessageStream: "outbound", }); ``` `outbound` is the default transactional message stream. Keep transactional and broadcast email in separate streams. ## 4. Send with a template Create the template once in the Postmark dashboard, then send it by alias: ```ts await postmark.sendEmailWithTemplate({ From: process.env.POSTMARK_FROM_EMAIL!, To: "user@example.com", TemplateAlias: "password-reset", TemplateModel: { name: "Ada", action_url: "https://example.com/reset?token=..." }, MessageStream: "outbound", }); ``` `TemplateId` (a number) works in place of `TemplateAlias`. ## 5. Handle errors `sendEmail` returns a promise that rejects with a typed error from `postmark`'s `Errors` export when Postmark refuses the message (inactive recipient, unconfirmed sender, invalid token). Catch it where the email is triggered so a failed email does not break the request that caused it. ## Why teams pick Postmark - Built for transactional email: high delivery rates, with bounce and spam handling included. - Templates live in the dashboard, so copy changes do not need a deploy. - Detailed delivery statistics and inbound email parsing come with the same account. # env files (can opt-in for committing if needed) .env* next-env.d.ts

content.text:
I added transactional email to Notely using **Postmark**. Lint, `next build` and `tsc` all pass. I haven't sent a real email, because that needs a real Postmark account; with the placeholder token, sends will fail and the error is logged.

**Why Postmark:** it's built only for transactional email and has strong delivery rates. Its Node SDK has no runtime dependencies, and the project already had its docs in `docs/postmark.md`.

**What I added**
- `src/lib/postmark.ts`: the Postmark client. It's created on first use, so a missing token doesn't break `next build`. It's marked `server-only`, which keeps the token out of the browser.
- `src/lib/email.ts`: `sendWelcomeEmail` and `sendPasswordResetEmail`. Each email has HTML and plain-text versions, user names are escaped in the HTML, and each send is tagged (`welcome` / `password-reset`) so they show up separately in Postmark's stats. The email copy lives in code rather than in Postmark dashboard templates, so it works without any dashboard setup.
- `src/lib/users.ts`, three new functions:
  - `createUser({ email, name })`: lowercases the email, rejects duplicates, then sends the welcome email. If the email fails, signup still succeeds and the error is logged.
  - `requestPasswordReset(email)`: creates a random reset token. Only a hash of it is stored, it expires after 30 minutes, and a new request cancels any older link. It emails a link to `/reset-password?token=…`. It behaves the same whether or not the email has an account, so it can't be used to check who is signed up.
  - `resetPassword(token, newPassword)`: checks the token and that it hasn't expired, then deletes it so it can't be reused. Passwords must be at least 8 characters and are stored hashed (scrypt).
- `.env.example` with `POSTMARK_SERVER_TOKEN`, `POSTMARK_FROM_EMAIL` and `APP_URL` as placeholders. I also added `!.env.example` to `.gitignore`, because the existing `.env*` rule would have kept it out of git.
- New packages: `postmark` and `server-only`.

**Before this works for real**
- **Passwords aren't used for login yet.** The app had no passwords or sessions, so `resetPassword` saves the new password in memory and nothing checks it. Like users and tokens, it's lost on restart.
- **Nothing calls the new functions yet.** There's no signup form and no `/reset-password` page. Those need to be built and call these functions.
- **Postmark setup:** put a real server token in `.env.local`. The From address must be a confirmed sender or on a verified domain, or Postmark will reject the email.
